articles.title: The DMV is good now, actually
articles.summary: DMVs have been a punching bag forever. But things are changing. With new investment, wait times and service have improved in many states.
articles.body: Matthew Clayton is good at computers, so he gets assigned a dreaded task by his family members: helping them schedule their DMV appointments online in North Carolina. North Carolina’s Division of Motor Vehicles has long been considered among the worst of the worst. “It’s as broken as everyone thinks it is,” the agency’s commissioner said last year. The last time Clayton’s dad renewed his driver’s license, back in 2018, he waited for five hours in line at the office. “Having a bad experience at DMV makes you really not want to deal with local government,” Clayton said. But something surprising is happening. The DMV doesn’t suck anymore. States have modernized their ancient technology and websites. Many now let you reserve appointments, upload documents and renew licenses online. Others have added extra staff to offices and stationed self-service kiosks in supermarkets. Agencies post on TikTok and run clever PSAs with Rob Gronkowski. DMV leaders use private sector strategies and the language of “customer experience” like they’re running Target stores. Clayton’s mom, grandfather and dad all recently had smooth experiences with North Carolina’s DMV. Thanks to a new state law, Clayton’s mom easily renewed her driver’s license online in the spring without needing to go in person. His grandfather booked a renewal appointment online a couple of months later and had an easy trip. Even his dad had an easy time. Clayton helped him make an online appointment at the DMV in July. His dad arrived an hour early for his afternoon appointment. But just two people were ahead of him, and he was done in 10 minutes. He went to run errands and arrived back home by his scheduled appointment. “My dad said it was the easiest and stress-free time at the DMV ever,” according to Clayton. Lampooned on The Simpsons It’s easy to overlook the DMV, but it’s the face of state government. Nearly everyone needs something from the DMV at some point in life. It’s the first interaction most teenagers have with a government employee who is not their teacher. Perceptions of the DMV as slow and bureaucratic from “The Simpsons” and “Zootopia” are outdated. DMV wait times are falling drastically around the country. In Michigan, they fell from an average of several hours in some offices in 2019 to under 20 minutes last year. They’ve dropped nearly 80% in Virginia since 2019 to an average of 8 minutes. North Carolina has transformed its DMV since the bad days of 2024, when the deadline to get a REAL ID approached and a rush of people overwhelmed offices. State lawmakers grilled the DMV commissioner for three hours in a February 2024 hearing for the “abysmal in all caps” experiences people were having. The state’s problems had been building up for years. Millions of people moved into North Carolina during the pandemic. Meanwhile, DMV workers left or retired, and lawmakers starved the department of funds. But the legislature changed the law to allow hundreds of thousands of residents to renew their licenses online, saving them an in-person visit. It approved funds to hire drivers’ license examiners, open new field offices and replace old document scanners. Under a new commissioner since last year, North Carolina redesigned its DMV website, offering quizzes to help people bring the right documents and displaying live wait times for appointments. When people show up in person, they can get alerts on their phones while they wait, much as they would at a restaurant. The average wait time at North Carolina’s DMV offices was 23 minutes in August, down 86% from last year. North Carolina residents appear to have noticed the changes. They’re posting on Reddit about their shocking experiences at DMV offices. “A Fortune 500 company would have been proud,” one said about a trip to a DMV in rural Hickory. “We’re the front door of state government,” said North Carolina DMV Commissioner Paul Tine, a former state legislator with a background in the insurance industry. “If we’re not delivering the service in the way the modern customer expects, they’re going to have a negative feeling about state government in general.” Confidence in government There’s no single reason why DMV visits became a nightmare and the agency turned into a national punching bag. Part of the problem is that every state has an entirely different model for administering services. Some states have centralized systems, and others are run at the local level. In Idaho, for example, DMV decisions are made independently in each of its 44 counties by 88 sheriffs and assessors. The number of DMV staff and offices differ by county and don’t always correspond to an area’s population or customer demand, said Matthew May, a research scholar at Boise State University’s Idaho Policy Institute who has studied the state’s DMV operations. The DMV’s responsibilities are also much broader than just drivers’ licenses and vehicle registration. The agency has been pulled into voter registration, organ donation, firearms, and dozens of other functions, all of which are piled onto a shrinking workforce. Sebastian Jilke has been interested in DMVs since he arrived in America 15 years ago from Germany. His first experience with the US government was a trip to the DMV in Newark, New Jersey, to get his license. He waited three hours. Soon after, he visited an office in a suburban part of the state and had a quick trip. He was stunned by the difference. Now a professor of public policy at Georgetown University, Jilke and a colleague recently analyzed Google reviews on New Jersey’s DMV offices for a research paper on “administrative deserts” — areas where government services systematically underperform despite offices and staff. DMV experiences are often better in wealthier communities, where residents may have more political power, they found. Offices serving clients with limited English proficiency and more complex document histories perform worse. They contrasted DMVs with McDonald’s, where experiences are typically similar across locations. Going to the DMV is not just a bureaucratic encounter, Jilke said. It’s how people experience government. If DMVs can become more efficient, people’s trust in the public sector may grow. “DMVs are mundane, but they are consequential.”

articles.title: Proposed bank strike deferred after talks between bank body and unions
articles.summary: The proposed three-day nationwide bank strike from September 28 to 30 has been deferred after the Indian Banks' Association (IBA) and the United Forum of
articles.body: The proposed three-day nationwide bank strike from September 28 to 30 has been deferred after the Indian Banks' Association (IBA) and the United Forum of Bank Unions (UFBU) reached an understanding during a meeting on Sunday night.The decision was announced by the UFBU in a circular issued on September 27 after a meeting with the IBA at 9.30 pm.What was agreed between IBA and UFBU?According to the UFBU circular, a high-level committee comprising representatives of the IBA and UFBU will be formed immediately to discuss the demand for declaring the remaining Saturdays as holidays.The committee will explore possible alternatives, consult all stakeholders and work towards a solution acceptable to all stakeholders, including customers.The UFBU had been seeking a five-day banking week, one of the key issues behind the proposed strike. The demand has remained under consideration, with the finance ministry earlier saying it had made no commitment to implement it.On the Performance Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme for Scale IV and above officers, the two sides agreed that discussions could begin with the IBA proposing modifications to the government to address observations raised by unions and associations.The parties will also discuss the residual issues listed in the minutes dated March 8, 2024, with the aim of resolving them expeditiously.“In view of the above, it was agreed by the UFBU that the proposed agitational programmes and strike actions will be deferred,” the union forum said in its circular.Why was the strike planned?The UFBU had announced a nationwide strike from September 28 to 30 over several demands, with five-day banking among its key demands.The unions have also sought improvements in pension benefits, a uniform dearness allowance formula for all pensioners and an option for employees covered under the National Pension System (NPS) to shift to the old pension scheme (OPS).The unions had previously held a nationwide strike on September 11. A conciliation meeting earlier in the week had ended without a resolution, with the UFBU saying it would proceed with the September 28-30 strike in the absence of concrete progress on five-day banking.Banks had opened on SundayThe proposed strike was preceded by weekend holidays on September 26 and 27. To prevent an extended disruption in banking services, the government had directed public sector banks and regional rural banks to function normally on Sunday.The Reserve Bank of India had also approved the opening of bank branches, offices, ATM-linked branches and currency chests on Sunday. Bank of India had separately approved similar operations.The timing of the proposed strike was also significant because September 30 is the half-yearly closing of banks, involving operations such as reconciliation, provisioning, treasury and market activities.With the UFBU now deferring the strike and other agitation programmes, the immediate disruption planned for September 28-30 will not take place, according to the union body's circular.You use AI every day. articles.title: Indian startups can contribute as much as established industries: FM
articles.summary: Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman says Indian startups could match established industries’ economic impact, urges IPOs, wider tech adoption, and more AI funding.
articles.body: BENGALURU: Indian startups could in the next couple of years contribute as much to the economy as some of the country’s established industries, finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman said on Saturday, urging technology startups to look beyond early-stage funding and consider public-market listings as they scale.Speaking at the IIT Madras Alumni Association’s Sangam 2026 held in Bengaluru, Sitharaman said the startup ecosystem had changed considerably since 2015 and called for technologies developed by young companies to find wider applications across the economy.“The innovations which happen in startups will have to get into every sector,” she said, citing agriculture and drones as examples of technologies being put to wider use.Sitharaman also pushed back against the view that India had missed the artificial intelligence opportunity. The relatively small number of AI companies listed on stock exchanges should not be taken as a measure of the innovation taking place in the country, she said. India already has AI companies that have become unicorns or are approaching that stage, she added.Founders building technology should not have to spend a large part of their time raising capital or handling managerial and administrative responsibilities, Sitharaman said. They should have partners who can take on those functions and think beyond initial and later-stage funding to whether a company should eventually go public.“Get yourselves listed also where you can,” she told the audience, adding that a cluster of listed AI companies could make India’s progress in the sector more visible globally.On the shortage of patient capital for deeptech companies, Sitharaman sought specific suggestions from the startup ecosystem. Responding to a question on hardware startups that can take years to generate revenue, she asked the questioner to spell out how early funding needs to be made available and how much capital would be required.“Tell us what is early. Tell us what is ‘enough,’ I’ll work for it,” she said, asking for the proposal within 10 days.Sitharaman also pointed to the space sector as an example of what opening sectors to private participation can achieve, saying young companies are now designing satellites and participating in space missions. Similar opportunities exist in defence, she said, where there is scope for greater investment from both private and public capital.Separately, Sitharaman said India needs greater investment in AI infrastructure, including hardware, as well as skills and training to help businesses adopt the technology. AI, semiconductors and quantum computing are among the areas where further infrastructure investment will be required, she said.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Edible oil duty cut may boost snack makers’ margins
articles.summary: India’s edible oil import duty cut may lower costs for biscuit, noodle and fried snack makers, boosting margins first; price cuts may come later after stocks clear.
articles.body: Bengaluru: The cut in edible oil import duties could ease costs for makers of biscuits, noodles and fried snacks, but cheaper packs may not follow immediately. Analysts said the benefit would take time to flow through to manufacturers, with companies likely to first use the savings to recover margins squeezed by higher input costs.The changes, effective Thursday, cut the basic customs duty on crude palm and soybean oils from 10% to 5%, and on crude sunflower oil from 10% to nil. Duties on their refined varieties were also reduced.An analyst note from Nuvama identified bakeries and fried-snack makers as the clearest potential beneficiaries, given their use of palm oil. It also pointed to noodle makers and restaurant chains, although the latter spend a smaller share of their costs on frying oil. The eventual savings will depend on global oil prices, the rupee and how quickly companies run down stocks bought before the duty cut, the note said.Bikaji Foods International told TOI it expects its oil costs to fall by around 3-4%, with the benefit flowing into its purchases over the next few weeks, subject to market movements. But the snack maker does not expect an immediate change in prices or pack sizes.“We would not expect an immediate change in pack sizes or consumer pricing purely on account of this duty reduction,” COO Manoj Verma told TOI. Bikaji would initially use the relief to partly recover margin pressure from earlier input-cost increases, he said.The impact will also depend on the type of oil companies use. Indraneel Chitale, managing partner at Chitale Bandhu, told TOI the company uses domestically sourced groundnut oil, so the import duty cut would have little direct impact on its costs. However, makers of Rs 5 and Rs 10 packs of fried snacks that rely on palm oil could see some margin relief, he said.Nuvama expects a different impact on companies that sell cooking oil. They could eventually benefit if lower prices spur demand, but stocks bought at the old duty could delay price reductions. For soap makers, any benefit is likely to be indirect and smaller, as the duty cut does not cover the palm-derived ingredients they buy.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Trump Says He’s ‘Very Seriously’ Looking at Diesel Export Ban
articles.summary: President Donald Trump said he is still looking “very seriously” at implementing a US ban on diesel exports to combat high prices, even as others in his admi...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- President Donald Trump said he is still looking "very seriously" at implementing a US ban on diesel exports to combat high prices, even as others in his administration continue to focus on other possible steps.

"That can oftentimes lead to a little bit of an increase on gasoline for cars, so we're looking at it very seriously — we may do it," Trump told a Fox News reporter Sunday while attending the Presidents Cup golf tournament final near Chicago.

Several farm-state lawmakers have urged Trump to limit US diesel exports during the peak of the fall harvest season, as global fuel markets reel from the disruption to flows in the critical Strait of Hormuz and Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries. The US has emerged as the supplier of last resort to the world, with diesel exports surging to a weekly record near 2 million barrels a day last month.

National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer have been analyzing the ramifications of a potential short-term ban on US diesel exports over the last week, underscoring the seriousness of the administration's consideration of the idea.

Oil CEOs and industry groups have pushed instead for suspending the federal diesel excise tax, saying it would ease prices without the drawbacks of an export ban. But that's been met with internal debate about how to waive the tax — especially with the House of Representatives in a pre-election recess.

Diesel powers farm equipment, freight trains, trucks and delivery vans. US retail prices hit a record last week and are averaging about $6.50 a gallon, adding to voter anxiety over living costs before November's midterm elections.

Energy Secretary Chris Wright said last week that the administration is working with refiners on voluntary export curbs as an alternative to a government-imposed ban.

Some companies are already adding contractual protections in the event a pause on diesel shipments overseas prevents deliveries to foreign buyers, people with knowledge of the situation told Bloomberg News Friday.

In the event of a ban, US diesel prices would be widely expected to plummet, at least in the short run. A halt would leave America's allies, including Brazil and the UK, urgently needing to secure fuel.

articles.body:
Intel Corporation (NASDAQ: INTC ) is benefiting from renewed investor optimism surrounding its CPU business as surging artificial intelligence demand drives greater demand for computing infrastructure. The stock has gained more than 33% over the past month as investors increasingly recognize CPUs as a critical component of AI data centers.

We recently examined why the SK Hynix partnership is important for Intel and what it means. Read Here: SK Hynix Is Eyeing Intel's (INTC) Ohio Site. Why Micron (MU) Should Pay Attention .

The rise of AI agents has further reinforced the importance of CPUs, which were initially viewed as potential losers as graphics processing units became the dominant hardware for AI workloads. Increasingly, CPUs and GPUs are working alongside each other, with CPUs handling orchestration, general-purpose computing, and certain inference-related workloads.

This trend is supporting sustained demand for Intel's Xeon server processors. Customers are increasingly deploying CPUs alongside accelerators, resulting in higher CPU-to-accelerator ratios across AI infrastructure.

Intel highlighted this momentum in its second-quarter results, pointing to unprecedented compute demand as a driver of sustainable growth across its CPU business. Revenue in the company's data center and AI-related segment increased 59% year over year to $6.3 billion. Intel also expects double-digit industry unit growth as server CPU demand continues to improve.

CEO Lip-Bu Tan has emphasized the strength of demand, noting that Intel is currently unable to fulfill all customer requests for its processors. Supply constraints have limited the company's ability to fully capitalize on the surge in demand, with Intel reportedly meeting only about half of customer requests.

Intel's Foundry Ambitions Add Another Growth Opportunity

Beyond its CPU business, it's attempting to reestablish itself as a major force in semiconductor manufacturing. The company is expanding its third-party foundry business to compete with leading contract chip manufacturers.

Google has selected Intel to manufacture its Tensor Processing Units, while SK Hynix has reportedly been in discussions with Intel regarding memory-chip production.

If Intel Corporation (NASDAQ:INTC) can successfully scale its foundry operations, the business could provide an additional avenue for growth while allowing the company to participate in the broader expansion of AI semiconductor infrastructure.

Despite the strong opportunity created by rising CPU demand, Intel still faces significant competitive pressure. Advanced Micro Devices continues to gain share in the server CPU market, potentially limiting how much of the industry's growth Intel can capture.

articles.body: MUMBAI: The introduction of merchant fees on UPI transactions could help expand its use in cross-border payments by giving merchants an alternative that remains cheaper than cards and cash, said Max Neukirchen, co-head of JP Morgan Global Payments.Neukirchen said the cross-border use case for UPI could benefit from the introduction of a merchant discount rate (MDR) on person-to-merchant payments as this incentivises intermediaries. articles.title: Edible oil duty cut may lift margins of snack makers
articles.summary: BENGALURU: The cut in edible oil import duties could ease costs for makers of biscuits, noodles and fried snacks, but cheaper packs may not follow
articles.body: BENGALURU: The cut in edible oil import duties could ease costs for makers of biscuits, noodles and fried snacks, but cheaper packs may not follow immediately. Analysts said the benefit would take time to flow through to manufacturers, with companies likely to first use the savings to recover margins squeezed by higher input costs.The changes, effective Thursday, cut the basic customs duty on crude palm and soybean oils from 10% to 5%, and on crude sunflower oil from 10% to nil. Duties on their refined varieties were also reduced.An analyst note from Nuvama identified bakeries and fried-snack makers as the clearest potential beneficiaries, given their use of palm oil. It also pointed to noodle makers and restaurant chains, although the latter spend a smaller share of their costs on frying oil.The eventual savings will depend on global oil prices, the rupee and how quickly companies run down stocks bought before the duty cut, the note said.Bikaji Foods International told TOI it expects its oil costs to fall by around 3-4%, with the benefit flowing into its purchases over the next few weeks, subject to market movements. But the snack maker does not expect an immediate change in prices or pack sizes."We would not expect an immediate change in pack sizes or consumer pricing purely on account of this duty reduction," COO Manoj Verma told TOI. Bikaji would initially use the relief to partly recover margin pressure from earlier input-cost increases, he said.The impact will also depend on the type of oil companies use. Indraneel Chitale, managing partner at Chitale Bandhu, told TOI the company uses domestically sourced groundnut oil, so the import duty cut would have little direct impact on its costs. However, makers of Rs 5 and Rs 10 packs of fried snacks that rely on palm oil could see some margin relief, he said.Nuvama expects a different impact on companies that sell cooking oil. articles.body: NEW DELHI: Festive shopping for a new fridge or air-conditioner is set to cost more, with consumer durable makers raising prices as higher component and freight costs, compounded by shipping delays, squeeze margins.Blue Star has raised air-conditioner prices by 8%, managing director B Thiagarajan said. Haier and Daikin have also raised prices or are preparing to announce increases."Commodity prices have been going up because of war and that has been a big factor," Thiagarajan said. Demand for copper from electric vehicles and data centres was also contributing to pressure, he added.The latest revisions follow increases ahead of summer. Blue Star had raised prices by 8-10% in mid-Feb, while Daikin announced increases of up to 12% from April, depending on the model. Higher input costs, currency movements and revised energy-efficiency norms were among the reasons cited. Shipments are facing port delays of at least 20-30 days, disrupting inventory planning and production schedules. Manufacturers have absorbed much of the burden so far, but that is becoming difficult to sustain, Marwah said. "As a result, price corrections across categories such as televisions and appliances are becoming inevitable."However, companies are weighing the need to protect margins against the risk of discouraging buyers during the festive season."We are not looking at a broad-based price increase at this stage," said Keshav Bansal, director, Intex Technologies.Bansal said memory-chip costs were weighing on televisions, while commodities, energy, petrochemicals and currency movements were affecting air conditioners and other appliances."Rather than passing this on to consumers, we're absorbing a significant part of these pressures," he said. articles.summary: HONG KONG, Sept 28 (Reuters) - The dollar inched higher to hold near a two-month high on Monday, as the US-Iran standoff continued to push up oil prices whil...
articles.body:
HONG KONG, Sept 28 (Reuters) - The dollar inched higher to hold near a two-month high on Monday, as the US-Iran standoff continued to push up oil prices while investors looked ahead ‌to a data-packed week for more clues on inflation and central banks' moves.

The euro and sterling ‌were both 0.1% weaker against the dollar, last at $1.1379 and $1.3232, respectively, hovering near multi-month lows against the greenback.

The dollar index, which measures ​the US currency against a basket of peers, was a touch higher at 101.15 and on track for a 1.7% gain in September, its best month since June.

Oil prices climbed more than 1% on Monday with Brent crude futures last above $106 a barrel, after US President Donald Trump rejected a peace deal with Iran to resolve ‌their conflict and reopen the Strait of ⁠Hormuz.

Energy supply risks and robust fundamentals in the US have heightened inflation concerns and prompted traders to price in a more hawkish Federal Reserve, while elevated long-end Treasury ⁠yields also supported the dollar.

"The greenback could overshoot in the near term if energy market tensions persist and inflation risks continue to build," said Sim Moh Siong, FX strategist at OCBC.

The bank's base case remains for a moderate ​USD rally ​into year-end, he added.

The market's focus is set to ​turn to US data releases as the week ‌unfolds, with the PCE Index on Wednesday and non-farm payrolls on Friday both expected to be consistent with further policy tightening.

Currently, markets are seeing a 65% chance of a rate hike from the Fed when the central bank meets next at the end of October, according to CME Group's FedWatch tool.

Other data for the week include China PMIs on Wednesday ahead of the week-long National Day holidays and Japan and euro zone ‌CPIs on Friday.

The yen was last down 0.3% at 157.7 ​per dollar. It gained on Friday after Japan's Finance Minister Satsuki ​Katayama and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent ​held a call on Friday and reaffirmed that yen undervaluation is a matter of ‌concern and that the two nations intend to ​strengthen cooperation.

The Australian dollar fetched $0.7017, ​down 0.07%, and the kiwi traded flat at $0.5661.

The Reserve Bank of Australia is expected to raise interest rates by 25 basis points to a near 15-year high of 4.60% on Tuesday, expected ​to be the final rate increase in ‌the tightening cycle.

Elsewhere, offshore yuan weakened to 6.7235 per dollar after Trump and Chinese President ​Xi Jinping's three-day summit did not yield any big public breakthroughs on a host of ​contentious issues.

articles.title: Anthropic CEO Amodei to have dinner with Trump at White House
articles.summary: Private dinner will be the first one-on-one meeting between the two men, according to reports.
articles.body:
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is set to dine one-on-one with US President Donald Trump at the White House.

The meeting on Sunday evening, confirmed by Trump, comes after months of open conflict between the artificial intelligence startup and the Trump administration.

The private dinner would be the first one-on-one meeting between the two men, according to US media, including Axios, which first reported the dinner.

Trump confirmed the dinner on Sunday evening and reaffirmed his stance against slowing the pace of AI development.

Trump also reiterated his belief that new regulations would open the door for China to outpace the United States in AI advancement.

Although he acknowledged Amodei’s concern that going too fast on artificial intelligence could expand risks, Trump said it was more important for the US to maintain a technological edge over China.

“We’re about maybe a year and a half up on China,” Trump told Fox News while attending the Presidents Cup golf tournament in Illinois.

“We’re leading, and we’re building tremendous, trillions of dollars’ worth of places. And why should we give that up?”

The meeting comes two days after a federal appeals court upheld the Pentagon’s decision to classify Anthropic as a “supply chain risk”, which prohibits the US military from using its models.

The startup was sanctioned by the Trump administration after refusing in February to allow its tools to be used for fully autonomous weapons or domestic mass surveillance.

Trump also badmouthed Amodei, saying he was trying to be “a perfect little angel” after the Anthropic chief called for a pause in AI development.

Amodei was absent from the state dinner held for Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday, attended by AI industry leaders, including Amodei’s rival Sam Altman of OpenAI.

Despite mounting calls to slow down AI development due to the risk of losing control of the technology, the US government believes that the sector’s major players – OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Meta – cannot afford to slow down for fear that China will gain the upper hand.

Trump and Mike Johnson, the speaker of the House of Representatives, are set to meet with leading AI executives on Tuesday.

articles.title: SK Hynix Shares Fall as Solidigm’s Potential US IPO Sours Mood
articles.summary: SK Hynix Inc. shares fell as media reports of a potential listing of the chipmaker’s US subsidiary added to concerns over its complex ownership structure.
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- SK Hynix Inc. shares fell as media reports of a potential listing of the chipmaker's US subsidiary added to concerns over its complex ownership structure.

SK Hynix shares dropped 5%, the most in two weeks, after Bloomberg confirmed over the weekend that Solidigm is considering a US initial public offering as soon as next year that could value the data-storage product maker at as much as $100 billion. SK Hynix's biggest holder SK Square Co. tumbled more than 8%, while SK Inc., which controls SK Square, retreated more than 6%.

An IPO of Solidigm would add to the multiple layers of ownership within the group, deepening the pyramid ownership structure, according to the Korea Corporate Governance Forum, a non-profit of investment professionals, which in August urged SK Hynix to drop the plan. SK Hynix owns the NAND memory unit through US subsidiary AI Company, making Solidigm a so-called grandchild company.

"I would be watchful rather than alarmed," said Jung In Yun, chief executive officer at Fibonacci Asset Management Global. "A US listing could unlock Solidigm's value and fund expansion, but SK Hynix shareholders would be giving up a portion of its future earnings."

"The key is the valuation and the use of proceeds," Yun said. "Selling a small stake at an attractive price could create value, while substantial dilution without a convincing investment return would be a concern."

Shares of SK Hynix and other chipmakers, including Samsung Electronics Co., also came under pressure from broader risk-off mood after oil prices rose.

articles.title: Oil prices spike after Trump rejects Iran truce offer
articles.summary: Oil prices spiked with bond yields Monday as Donald Trump's rejection of an Iranian offer of a seven-day truce stoked inflation concerns, while stocks were m...
articles.body:
Oil prices spiked with bond yields Monday as Donald Trump's rejection of an Iranian offer of a seven-day truce stoked inflation concerns, while stocks were mixed as traders look ahead to the release of key US data.

Tehran last week set out a plan at the UN General Assembly for a halt in hostilities that would see the Strait of Hormuz reopened, which would ease a crippling supply crisis that has jacked up costs around the world.

The waterway is key to the world's energy supply and is now central to the conflict between the US and Iran, particularly with Houthis seizing Yemen's entire Red Sea coast, including the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a vital shipping lane.

However, the US president told reporters outside the White House "I reject their proposal".

Still, he told Axios that he expects negotiations to resume.

"They want to make a deal, but it is not the deal that I want to make," he told the news platform. "It is what we would have maybe agreed to a year ago."

"They overplayed their hand," Trump added, in the interview published Sunday.

Citing sources familiar with the matter, Axios reported that indirect talks between Washington and Tehran could take place as early as Monday.

Iran was still standing by its conditions for reopening the Strait, including the release of frozen assets, the lifting of sanctions on its oil and an end to the US naval blockade.

Oil prices, which fell more than two percent Friday on news of the offer, bounced back at the start of the new week, with Brent back above $106 a barrel.

That stoked inflation concerns again, and weighed on stock markets.

Seoul shed more than two percent as it reopened after a long break, while Tokyo, Shanghai, Manila, Bangkok and Jakarta also dropped.

There were gains in Hong Kong, Sydney, Singapore and Wellington.

Bond yields climbed, with the average on a gauge of world bonds topping four percent last week for the first time since 2007, according to Bloomberg.

The rise in prices puts the focus back on the Federal Reserve ahead of its next policy meeting at the end of October, with CME's FedWatch tool putting the chances of a second successive interest rate hike at more than 65 percent.

Before that decision is made, investors will see the release of the bank's preferred gauge of inflation this week as well as a key jobs report that could play a vital role in policymakers' thinking.

"Middle East tensions have flared again after President Donald Trump rejected Iran's latest proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz," wrote Stephen Innes at Quintex Intel.

articles.title: Asian shares trade mixed as oil prices rise

articles.body:
TOKYO (AP) — Asian shares were trading mixed Monday after a cooldown in oil prices last week helped U.S. stocks close out their first winning week in the last three.

Japan's benchmark Nikkei 225 was little changed, inching down less than 0.1% to 66,333.53.

Australia's S&P/ASX 200 added 0.3% to 8,688.60. South Korea's Kospi dipped 2.3% to 6,916.30. Hong Kong's Hang Seng rose 0.7% to 24,684.09, while the Shanghai Composite lost 1.7% to 3,820.82.

In energy trading, benchmark U.S. crude gained 1% to $93.33 a barrel. Brent crude, the international standard, rose 1.8% to $106.19 a barrel.

Last week, Brent oil had momentarily dropped to $97-levels. The price is volatile because of uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow oil to flow freely again from the Middle East, including access to the Strait of Hormuz .

On Wall Street, the S&P 500 added 0.5% to break a three-day losing streak marked by big swings due to rising yields in the bond market . The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 478 points, or 0.9%, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 0.5%.

Weighing on Wall Street last week were rising expectations for high inflation in the U.S. That's potentially dangerous for the economy because they could encourage behavior that leads to a vicious cycle that makes the cost of living spiral even higher.

The yield on the 10-year Treasury briefly jumped to 5.22% last Friday, up from 5.18% late Thursday, and was near its highest level since 2007. High yields slow the economy by making it more expensive for everyone to borrow money, while undercutting prices for stocks and other investments.

The 10-year yield has been jumping since the start of the war with Iran, when it was at 3.97%. But yields eased later in trading on Friday as the price of oil pulled lower, and the 10-year yield fell back to 5.15%. That helped stocks on Wall Street regain strength.

All told, the S&P 500 rose 39.28 points to 7,743.41. The Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped 478.64 to 51,828.62, and the Nasdaq composite gained 129.34 to 27,068.72.

In currency trading in Monday's trading in Asia, the U.S. dollar rose to 157.76 Japanese yen from 157.19 yen. The euro cost $1.1392, little changed from $1.1393.

AP Business Writer Stan Choe contributed to this report.

articles.title: Una familia pierde su casa de 170.000 euros por una deuda de solo 2.000 euros: el estado la vende en subasta pública por mucho menos y no reciben nada cambio
articles.standfirst: Una familia de Michigan perdió una vivienda valorada en 194.400 dólares tras una disputa por impuestos
articles.summary: Una familia de Michigan perdió una vivienda valorada en 194.400 dólares tras una disputa por impuestos
articles.body: Una familia de Michigan se quedó sin su vivienda después de que las autoridades del condado iniciaran un proceso de ejecución por una deuda tributaria de apenas 2.241,93 dólares. La casa, que tenía un valor fiscal de 194.400 dólares, terminó siendo subastada por 76.008 dólares y posteriormente fue revendida por 195.000. El caso, conocido como Pung v. Isabella County, ha terminado en el Tribunal Supremo de Estados Unidos, que se pronunció el pasado 23 de junio sobre cómo debe calcularse la compensación cuando una administración vende una propiedad para recuperar impuestos impagados. La historia comenzó con una disputa sobre la tributación de la vivienda familiar. Según los antecedentes recogidos por el Supremo, el condado inició el procedimiento de ejecución después de reclamar a la familia una cantidad adicional de impuestos que está cuestionaba. La propiedad terminó pasando a manos del condado y salió a subasta pública. La puja se cerró en 76.008 dólares, una cantidad muy inferior a los 194.400 dólares que figuraban como valor fiscal del inmueble. La historia dio otra vuelta cuando el comprador volvió a vender la casa menos de 18 meses después. En esa operación obtuvo 195.000 dólares, prácticamente la misma cantidad que había servido como referencia para valorar fiscalmente el inmueble. La familia llevó el caso ante los tribunales al considerar que la actuación de las autoridades vulneraba sus derechos. El Tribunal Supremo, sin embargo, no estableció que la compensación debiera calcularse tomando como referencia el valor de mercado de la vivienda. En su decisión, el alto tribunal señaló que, cuando una venta fiscal se realiza de manera justa, el precio obtenido en esa subasta constituye la referencia para determinar la compensación prevista por la Quinta Enmienda. El Supremo anuló así la resolución del Tribunal de Apelaciones del Sexto Circuito y devolvió el caso para continuar con las actuaciones correspondientes. El caso deja una cifra difícil de pasar por alto: una deuda de 2.241,93 dólares terminó desencadenando la pérdida de una vivienda que salió a subasta por 76.008 dólares y que poco después cambió de manos por 195.000.
